newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries close up on signs of slower economy.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries close up on signs of slower economy.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices finished higher on Thursday after the government released more data showing that the economy slowed in September.
Regarding housing activity, the government said new housing starts fell six percent to an annualized 1.438 million in September from a revised 1.529 million in August.
The Federal Reserve then reported that industrial production rose just 0.2 percent in September after a moderate 0.4 percent increase in August.

The percentage of the nation's mines, factories and utilites engaged in that production -- the Fed refers to that as capacity utilization -- edged down to 83.3 in September, from a revised 83.4 percent in August.
Two October reports on economic activity indicated that the slowing trend persisted into the current month as well.
In the labor market, new claims for unemployment insurance jumped by 18,000 to 340,000 in the week ended October 12, the Labor Department said.
And the Philadelphia Fed's survey of regional business activity fell to -5.3 in October from 13.9 in September.

Coming after Wednesday's news that the Consumer Price Index rose only 0.3 percent in September, the data released on Thursday increased investors' confidence in the outlook for a moderate-growth, low-inflation economy, analysts said.

"It was a great day for bonds as investors clearly responded to a bank of bond-friendly economic data," said William Sullivan, senior vice president and economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc. "The data gave the market a higher comfort level with the theme that the Fed is fashioning a moderation in overall economic activity that will remain free of inflationary pressures."
The warmly received data pulled buyers off the sidelines.

"The market saw some respectable retail interest that helped prices move higher and yields lower," said Steve Ricchuito, chief financial economist at BZW Securities Inc. "Accounts are back to neutral and going a little bit long."
"There was a steady stream of buyers along the curve and the market closed at its highs," said Sullivan.
The 6-3/4 percent 30-year benchmark Treasury bond ended at 98-11/32, up 24/32, to yield 6.80 percent, versus 6.86 percent at Wednesday's close.

The bond market's gain came alongside the dollar's, which rose sharply against the mark in the foreign exchange markets after Russian President Boris Yeltsin fired his security chief Alexander Lebed, criticizing him for acting independently and splitting Russia's leadership team.
Dollar strength was "related to rumors (on Wednesday) of a Lebed coup and his subsequent demise," said Sullivan.

But the main driving factors for the bond market were the economic numbers, said Ricchuito, "in particular the decline in housing starts and the Philadelphia Fed number. Those two reports really motivated the market to go to higher levels."

At the short end of the maturity curve, three-month bill rates fell three basis points to 4.97 percent. Six-month bill rates fell four basis points to 5.08 percent. And year-bill rates fell six basis points to 5.21 percent.
"People's view of monetary policy has shifted from 'no interest-rate move in November but maybe one in December' to 'no move in November or December,'" Ricchuito said.

The two-year note ended at 100-8/32, up 3/32, to yield 5.86 percent. Five-year notes ended at 100-18/32, up 7/32, to yield 6.24 percent. The ten-year note closed at 99-31/32, up 13/32, to yield 6.50 percent. -- 212-859-1679
